label: Mo’edim Reference — Appointed Times, Preparation & Observance
summary_plain: The appointed times of the 364-day covenant calendar, each one given with its ancient name in paleo-Hebrew, the day it falls, what it is, what to gather beforehand, and what to do. Every appointed time begins at sunrise and ends at sunrise the next morning, so the window to prepare is the night before, up to dawn. The covenant record marks an appointed time three ways: Mo'ed, an appointed time; Miqra Qodesh, a set-apart assembly; Shabbaton, total cessation. Where the primary sources give no prayer text, that is said plainly — nothing is missing, there simply is not one.
summary_scholarly: The Mo'edim as fixed in the 364-day solar reckoning attested at Qumran (4QCalendrical Texts 4Q320-330), the Temple Scroll (11Q19), Yovelim, and the Ge'ez Orit. Each entry carries its date in the covenant calendar, the preparation the primary sources specify, the observance itself, and the textual notes governing it. The operative day boundary throughout is sunrise to sunrise per the DSS/Orit solar reckoning, against the sunset-to-sunset reckoning that follows Babylonian practice. Ancient names are given in unpointed paleo-Hebrew with English alongside; where no ancient Hebrew name for a day is attested in the DSS/Orit material, none is supplied and the omission is stated.

key_terms.definition: 𐤌𐤅𐤏𐤃 — Mo'ed — Appointed Time (Vayikra 23:2). One of the three ways the covenant record marks an appointed time. Source: DSS / Orit.
𐤌𐤒𐤓𐤀 𐤒𐤃𐤔 — Miqra Qodesh — Set-Apart Assembly. One of the three ways the covenant record marks an appointed time. Source: DSS / Orit.
𐤔𐤁𐤕𐤅𐤍 — Shabbaton — Total Cessation. One of the three ways the covenant record marks an appointed time. Source: DSS / Orit.

key_terms.term: The Day Boundary — Sunrise to Sunrise
key_terms.definition: Every appointed time begins at sunrise and ends at sunrise the following morning. The verse itself is rendered "evening to evening," but the operative day boundary followed here is sunrise to sunrise, per the DSS/Orit solar reckoning (Yovelim 3:28, 21:10, Vayikra 7:15, 22:29-30, Shemot 12:10, 23:18, 29:34, 34:25, Bamidbar 9:12, Devarim 16:4, 4QCalendrical Texts 4Q320-330) - sunset-to-sunset reckoning follows the Babylonian lunisolar calendar adopted by Rabbinic tradition after the exile, which the DSS community and the Orit Ge'ez did not follow.

Because the day begins at sunrise, the window to prepare for an appointed time runs through the night before, up to dawn. Whatever an appointed time calls for is gathered and set ready before first light.

𐤓𐤀𐤔 𐤇𐤃𐤔𐤉𐤌 — Rosh Chodashim — Shemot 12:2 — First day of the first month — Creation of Light — Beginning of the sacred year in the 364-day solar calendar. Attested in 4QCalendrical Text A. Month 1, Day 1 of the 364-day covenant calendar (the first month). Begins at sunrise; ends at sunrise the next morning. Source: DSS.

key_terms.term: New Year — Rosh Chodashim — What to Get Ready
key_terms.definition: Nothing to purchase. No individual ritual is attested for this day beyond the calendar reckoning itself.

key_terms.term: New Year — Rosh Chodashim — What to Do
key_terms.definition: 1. Confirm the new year's priestly course assignments (4Q320-330). 2. No fast, feast, or work-prohibition is specified for this day in the primary sources.

key_terms.term: New Year — Rosh Chodashim — Worth Knowing
key_terms.definition: The DSS calendrical texts (4Q320-330) use this day only to fix the priestly course rotation and anchor the 364-day/52-week cycle - no distinct ritual for the day itself is attested beyond that reckoning. Prepare by confirming the new year's course assignments; there is no fast, feast, or work-prohibition specified in the primary sources for this day. No prayer text specific to this day survives among the DSS/Orit primary sources.

𐤐𐤎𐤇 — Pesach — Preparation day — The 14th of the first month at evening. Slaughter of the Passover lamb. Confirmed in the Temple Scroll (11Q19) and 4QMMT. Month 1, Day 14 of the 364-day covenant calendar (the first month). Kept as: 𐤌𐤅𐤏𐤃 Mo'ed — Appointed Time (Vayikra 23:2). Begins at sunrise; ends at sunrise the next morning. Source: DSS/Orit.

key_terms.term: Pesach Eve — What to Get Ready
key_terms.definition: Gathered before sunrise: Unleavened flour and water, or store-bought matzah, enough for the week ahead; A roasted-meat meal (a modern stand-in for the sanctuary offering, not textually specified).

1. Before sunrise on the 15th, search the home and remove every leavened product - bread, crackers, pasta, beer. 2. At evening (twilight) on the 14th, the Passover lamb is slaughtered (Temple Scroll 11Q19 col. 17; 4QMMT). 3. Ensure no leaven remains once the seven days of Unleavened Bread begin at sunrise on the 15th.

Temple Scroll 11Q19 col. 17 and 4QMMT place the lamb's slaughter at evening (twilight). Prepare beforehand by removing all leaven from the household (Shemot 12:15,19) so none remains once the seven days of Unleavened Bread begin at sunrise on the 15th. No prayer text specific to this evening survives in the primary sources; Temple Scroll and 4QMMT describe the offering itself, not words recited over it.

𐤇𐤂 𐤄𐤌𐤑𐤅𐤕 — Chag HaMatzot — Passover — First day of the Festival of Unleavened Bread. The night of the Exodus from Egypt. Seven-day festival begins. Month 1, Day 15 of the 364-day covenant calendar (the first month). Kept as: 𐤌𐤅𐤏𐤃 Mo'ed — Appointed Time (Vayikra 23:2); 𐤌𐤒𐤓𐤀 𐤒𐤃𐤔 Miqra Qodesh — Set-Apart Assembly. Begins at sunrise; ends at sunrise the next morning. Source: DSS/Orit.

key_terms.term: Pesach — First Day — What to Get Ready
key_terms.definition: Gathered before sunrise: Matzah or homemade unleavened bread to last the full week; Wine or grape juice and bitter herbs (horseradish, romaine) - common modern additions, not DSS/Orit-attested.

key_terms.term: Pesach — First Day — What to Do
key_terms.definition: 1. Begin eating unleavened bread this evening and continue for the full seven days. 2. Keep this night as a night of watching, commemorating the Exodus. 3. Observe a sacred assembly with no ordinary work (Vayikra 23:7-8).

A sacred assembly with no ordinary work (Vayikra 23:7-8), elaborated in Temple Scroll's Temple-offering columns. Eat unleavened bread for the full seven days beginning this evening; the night itself commemorates the Exodus and is kept as a night of watching. No festival-specific prayer text for this day survives among the primary sources.

𐤇𐤂 𐤄𐤌𐤑𐤅𐤕 — Chag HaMatzot — Final day of Passover — Crossing of the Sea of Reeds. End of the Festival of Unleavened Bread. Confirmed in 4QCalendrical Text. Month 1, Day 21 of the 364-day covenant calendar (the first month). Kept as: 𐤌𐤅𐤏𐤃 Mo'ed — Appointed Time (Vayikra 23:2); 𐤌𐤒𐤓𐤀 𐤒𐤃𐤔 Miqra Qodesh — Set-Apart Assembly. Begins at sunrise; ends at sunrise the next morning. Source: DSS/Orit.

key_terms.term: Pesach — Seventh Day — What to Get Ready
key_terms.definition: Gathered before sunrise: Nothing new - continue the unleavened bread already on hand.

key_terms.term: Pesach — Seventh Day — What to Do
key_terms.definition: 1. Keep the closing sacred assembly of the Unleavened Bread week (Vayikra 23:8). 2. Continue avoiding leaven through the end of this day. 3. Set aside ordinary work again for the assembly.

Closing sacred assembly of the Unleavened Bread week (Vayikra 23:8), attested in the DSS calendrical texts as the festival's formal end. No leaven is eaten through this day; ordinary work is again set aside for the assembly. No festival-specific prayer text for this day survives among the primary sources.

𐤉𐤅𐤌 𐤄𐤍𐤐𐤄 — Yom HaNafah — Wave sheaf offering — The Sunday after the full Pesach week. The 26th of the first month. Beginning of the count toward Shavuot. Confirmed in 11Q19 Temple Scroll. Month 1, Day 26 of the 364-day covenant calendar (the first month). Kept as: 𐤌𐤅𐤏𐤃 Mo'ed — Appointed Time (Vayikra 23:2). Begins at sunrise; ends at sunrise the next morning. Source: DSS.

key_terms.term: First Fruits of Barley — What to Get Ready
key_terms.definition: Gathered before sunrise: Relevant mainly to those growing grain: the first cut of the barley harvest, set aside; Most households have nothing to purchase for this day.

key_terms.term: First Fruits of Barley — What to Do
key_terms.definition: 1. On the Sunday following the Pesach week, bring the wave-sheaf offering (Vayikra 23:10-14). 2. Do not eat, parch, or crush any new grain of the harvest until this offering is made.

key_terms.term: First Fruits of Barley — Worth Knowing
key_terms.definition: The wave-sheaf offering (Vayikra 23:10-14), anchored by the Qumran calendar specifically to the Sunday following the Pesach week - the community's own reading of "the day after the Sabbath," distinct from later reckonings that count from the first Pesach day itself (11Q19). No new grain of the harvest may be eaten, parched, or crushed until this offering is made. Temple Scroll describes the wave-sheaf offering itself but preserves no accompanying words recited over it.

𐤐𐤎𐤇 𐤔𐤍𐤉 — Pesach Sheni — Second Passover — For those who were ritually impure or on a distant journey during the first Pesach. Attested in DSS calendrical texts. Month 2, Day 15 of the 364-day covenant calendar (the second month). Kept as: 𐤌𐤅𐤏𐤃 Mo'ed — Appointed Time (Vayikra 23:2). Begins at sunrise; ends at sunrise the next morning. Source: DSS/Orit.

key_terms.term: Pesach Sheni — What to Get Ready
key_terms.definition: Gathered before sunrise: Matzah or unleavened bread; A roasted-meat meal, if marking it that way.
1. Applies only to those ritually impure or on a distant journey during the first Pesach (Bamidbar 9:9-13). 2. Keep the Pesach meal on this night instead of the original date.

The Torah's provision for those ritually impure or on a distant journey during the first Pesach (Bamidbar 9:9-13) - the DSS calendrical texts fix it as a standing date in the 364-day scheme rather than an occasional exception. Those it applies to keep the Pesach meal on this night instead. No prayer text specific to this day survives among the primary sources.

𐤇𐤂 𐤄𐤔𐤁𐤏𐤅𐤕 — Chag HaShavuot — Feast of Weeks — 50 days from the First Fruits offering. Revelation at Sinai. First Fruits of the Wheat harvest. One of the three pilgrimage festivals. Confirmed in 4Q319-330. Month 3, Day 15 of the 364-day covenant calendar (the third month). Kept as: 𐤌𐤅𐤏𐤃 Mo'ed — Appointed Time (Vayikra 23:2); 𐤌𐤒𐤓𐤀 𐤒𐤃𐤔 Miqra Qodesh — Set-Apart Assembly. Begins at sunrise; ends at sunrise the next morning. Source: DSS/Orit.

key_terms.term: Shavuot — Feast of Weeks — What to Get Ready
key_terms.definition: Gathered before sunrise: Two loaves of leavened bread (Temple Scroll 11Q19) - the one point in the calendar where leavened bread is specifically called for.

key_terms.term: Shavuot — Feast of Weeks — What to Do
key_terms.definition: 1. Prepare through self-examination before the gathering. 2. Bring the firstfruits of the wheat harvest, fifty days from the wave-sheaf (Vayikra 23:15-21). 3. Assemble for the Covenant Renewal ceremony (1QS I:16-II:18, II:19): purification, then passing member by member, by rank, into the renewed covenant. 4. Hear the blessings pronounced over "the men of the lot of the Creator" and the curses on the lot of Belial. 5. Answer "Amen, Amen" with the whole assembly.

key_terms.term: Shavuot — Feast of Weeks — Worth Knowing
key_terms.definition: Firstfruits of the wheat harvest, fifty days from the wave-sheaf (Vayikra 23:15-21), confirmed at this fixed date in 4Q319-330. At Qumran this was also the day of the annual Covenant Renewal ceremony (1QS I:16-II:18, II:19): the community assembled, was ritually purified, and passed - member by member, by rank - into the renewed covenant, with blessings pronounced over "the men of the lot of the Creator" and curses on the lot of Belial, the whole assembly answering "Amen, Amen." Prepare through self-examination before the gathering; the day itself is kept as a pilgrimage assembly, not a private one. Of these 22 days, this is one of the only two with an actual attested prayer text (the covenant liturgy described above) rather than just a description of the ritual - most of the others have none preserved. The Orit's own Jubilees 6 independently names this day as the anniversary of Noah's covenant oath after the flood, the origin it gives for the festival itself.

𐤕𐤒𐤅𐤐𐤄 — Tekufah — Seasonal marker — 91st day of the solar year. The turning point into summer. Not counted in the weekly cycle. Intercalary day unique to the 364-day DSS calendar. Month 3, Day 31 of the 364-day covenant calendar (the third month). Begins at sunrise; ends at sunrise the next morning. Source: DSS.

key_terms.term: Summer Tekufah — What to Get Ready
key_terms.definition: Nothing to purchase. A calendar turning-point only.
1. Mark the 91st day of the solar year, the turning point into summer. 2. No observance beyond the calendrical reckoning itself is attested - this day falls outside the seven-day week entirely.

A structural turning-point, not a festival - the 91st day, marking the solar year's move into summer. It falls outside the seven-day week entirely (4Q319, the Otot text, tracks these four turning points precisely to keep the 364-day/52-week scheme aligned). The Astronomical Book of Chanokh (Ch. 40) names this class of day directly: the year is twelve 30-day months (360 days) plus four separate days - this is the first of them - that "divide the four portions of the year" and are "not reckoned in the reckoning of the year," set apart under their own angelic custodians rather than folded into any month's day-count. No observance beyond the calendrical reckoning itself is attested. No prayer is attested for this day; it is a calendrical marker, not a liturgical one.

First day of the summer season. Beginning of the second quarter of the solar year. Month 4, Day 1 of the 364-day covenant calendar (the fourth month). Begins at sunrise; ends at sunrise the next morning. Source: DSS.

key_terms.term: New Season — Summer — What to Get Ready
key_terms.definition: Nothing to purchase.

key_terms.term: New Season — Summer — What to Do
key_terms.definition: 1. Mark the start of the year's second quarter. 2. No ritual requirement is attested for this day in the primary sources.

The start of the year's second quarter. Like the Tekufah before it, this is a calendrical marker in the DSS reckoning rather than a day with its own ritual requirement in the primary sources. No prayer is attested for this day.

New Wine offering — Festival of the first wine of the summer harvest. Fifty days after Shavuot in the Temple Scroll's (11Q19) sequential wave-offering count, falling on the 3rd of the 5th month. Month 5, Day 3 of the 364-day covenant calendar (the fifth month). Begins at sunrise; ends at sunrise the next morning. Source: DSS.

key_terms.term: Festival of New Wine — What to Get Ready
key_terms.definition: Gathered before sunrise: A bottle of wine, for a household blessing or libation (a practical stand-in, not the rite itself).

key_terms.term: Festival of New Wine — What to Do
key_terms.definition: 1. Fifty days after Shavuot, pour out new wine as a libation at the altar (Temple Scroll 11Q19 19:11-21:10). 2. Share the sacred meal in order: priests first, then Levites, then laypeople.

key_terms.term: Festival of New Wine — Worth Knowing
key_terms.definition: Fifty days after Shavuot, the second of the Temple Scroll's three sequential firstfruits festivals (11Q19 19:11-21:10). New wine is poured out as a libation at the altar; the sacred meal that follows is eaten first by the priests, then the Levites, then the laypeople, in that order. Temple Scroll (11Q19 19:11-21:10) describes the libation and the priests-then-Levites-then-laity meal order, but preserves no spoken blessing or prayer text for the occasion.

New Oil offering — Festival of the first olive oil pressed from the summer harvest. Confirmed in 4Q327 Calendrical Text. Falls on the 22nd of the 6th month. Month 6, Day 22 of the 364-day covenant calendar (the sixth month). Begins at sunrise; ends at sunrise the next morning. Source: DSS.

key_terms.term: Festival of New Oil — What to Get Ready
key_terms.definition: Gathered before sunrise: A bottle of olive oil, ideally fresh-pressed if available.

key_terms.term: Festival of New Oil — What to Do
key_terms.definition: 1. Fifty days after New Wine, bring a half-hin of freshly pressed oil per clan (Temple Scroll 11Q19 21:12-23:2). 2. Use part of the oil to anoint the lampstand and part as an atonement offering. 3. Do not use any oil of the new harvest until this offering is made.

key_terms.term: Festival of New Oil — Worth Knowing
key_terms.definition: Fifty days after New Wine (11Q19 21:12-23:2). Each clan brings a half-hin of freshly pressed oil - part used to anoint the lampstand, part offered as atonement. No oil of the new harvest is used until this offering is made, mirroring the wave-sheaf's rule for grain. Temple Scroll (11Q19 21:12-23:2) describes the clan offerings themselves; no accompanying prayer text is preserved.

𐤒𐤓𐤁𐤍 𐤄𐤏𐤑𐤉𐤌 — Qorban HaEtzim — Six-day Wood Offering festival begins. The community brings wood for the altar. Temple Scroll (11Q19) devotes extensive detail to this festival. Runs through the 28th of the 6th month. Month 6, Day 23 of the 364-day covenant calendar (the sixth month). Begins at sunrise; ends at sunrise the next morning. Source: DSS.

key_terms.term: Wood Offering — Day 1 — What to Get Ready
key_terms.definition: Gathered before sunrise: Firewood or kindling, if you have a fireplace, fire pit, or grill.

key_terms.term: Wood Offering — Day 1 — What to Do
key_terms.definition: 1. Prepare wood in advance of your assigned day in the clan rotation. 2. Bring wood to keep the altar fire supplied - this six-day festival runs through the 28th of the 6th month (Temple Scroll 11Q19 23:2-7).

A six-day festival (11Q19 23:2-7) in which the community brings wood to keep the altar fire supplied, apportioned across the days by clan rotation. Prepare wood in advance of one's assigned day; the offering itself is the day's whole observance. No prayer text is preserved for this offering in the primary sources.

𐤕𐤒𐤅𐤐𐤄 — Tekufah — Seasonal marker — 182nd day of the solar year. The turning point into autumn. Intercalary day unique to the 364-day DSS calendar. Month 6, Day 31 of the 364-day covenant calendar (the sixth month). Begins at sunrise; ends at sunrise the next morning. Source: DSS.

key_terms.term: Autumn Tekufah — What to Get Ready
key_terms.definition: Nothing to purchase.

1. Mark the 182nd day of the solar year, the turning point into autumn. 2. Keep the day as a matter of covenant faithfulness (Chanokh Ch. 75) rather than a minor scheduling detail - no ritual of its own is attested.

The 182nd day - the solar year's turning point into autumn, tracked the same way as the Summer Tekufah in 4Q319. Chanokh Ch. 75 frames failing to observe these four days as men going "wrong therein" in their reckoning of times and seasons - covenant faithfulness, not a minor scheduling detail, is what the text ties to keeping this day. A calendrical marker, not a day of its own ritual. No prayer is attested for this day; a calendrical marker only.

𐤉𐤅𐤌 𐤕𐤓𐤅𐤏𐤄 — Yom Teru'ah — Day of Trumpet Blasts — First day of the seventh month. Autumn New Year. Beginning of the third quarter of the solar year. Major festival of alarm and gathering. Month 7, Day 1 of the 364-day covenant calendar (the seventh month). Kept as: 𐤌𐤅𐤏𐤃 Mo'ed — Appointed Time (Vayikra 23:2); 𐤌𐤒𐤓𐤀 𐤒𐤃𐤔 Miqra Qodesh — Set-Apart Assembly; 𐤔𐤁𐤕𐤅𐤍 Shabbaton — Total Cessation. Begins at sunrise; ends at sunrise the next morning. Source: DSS/Orit.

key_terms.term: Yom Teruah — What to Get Ready
key_terms.definition: Gathered before sunrise: A shofar, ram's horn, or any wind instrument capable of a sustained blast.

1. At sunrise, sound the trumpet blast (Teru'ah) - the day's central act (Vayikra 23:24-25). 2. Set aside ordinary work for the full day. 3. This marks the start of the year's third quarter and the autumn new year in the DSS reckoning.

A day of trumpet blasts and gathering (Vayikra 23:24-25), marking the start of the year's third quarter and functioning as the autumn civil new year in the DSS reckoning. Ordinary work is set aside; the blasts themselves are the day's central act, calling the community to attention before the Day of Atonement ten days later. Vayikra 23:24 calls this a memorial of trumpet blasts - the blasts themselves are the day's central act; no separate prayer text is specified in the primary sources.

𐤉𐤅𐤌 𐤄𐤊𐤐𐤅𐤓𐤉𐤌 — Yom HaKippurim — Day of Atonement — The tenth of the seventh month. The High Priest enters the Holy of Holies. Complete fast from sunrise to sunrise. The most solemn day of the sacred year. Confirmed across all DSS legal texts. Month 7, Day 10 of the 364-day covenant calendar (the seventh month). Kept as: 𐤌𐤅𐤏𐤃 Mo'ed — Appointed Time (Vayikra 23:2); 𐤌𐤒𐤓𐤀 𐤒𐤃𐤔 Miqra Qodesh — Set-Apart Assembly; 𐤔𐤁𐤕𐤅𐤍 Shabbaton — Total Cessation. Begins at sunrise; ends at sunrise the next morning. Source: DSS/Orit.

key_terms.term: Yom Kippur — What to Get Ready
key_terms.definition: Nothing to purchase - this is a complete fast from sunrise to sunrise. The preparation is clearing one's calendar and settling ordinary matters beforehand, not acquiring anything.

1. Before sunrise, settle all ordinary matters and calendar obligations. 2. At sunrise, begin the complete fast and total rest - self-affliction (inui nefesh), the Torah's own phrase (Vayikra 16, 23:26-32). 3. Eat, drink, and work at nothing for the full day. 4. No fixed confession wording survives in the DSS for the High Priest's role (Vayikra 16:21 describes its content, not exact words; the well-known Hebrew confession is Mishnaic and isn't used here). 5. Continue the fast without interruption through the following sunrise, when it ends.

The most solemn day of the sacred year (Vayikra 16, 23:26-32), elaborated in Temple Scroll cols. 25-27: the High Priest enters the Holy of Holies, and the day is kept as a complete fast and total rest for the full day - self-affliction (inui nefesh), the Torah's own phrase. The verse itself is rendered "evening to evening," but the operative day boundary followed here is sunrise to sunrise, per the DSS/Orit solar reckoning (Yovelim 3:28, 21:10, Vayikra 7:15, 22:29-30, Shemot 12:10, 23:18, 29:34, 34:25, Bamidbar 9:12, Devarim 16:4, 4QCalendrical Texts 4Q320-330) - sunset-to-sunset reckoning follows the Babylonian lunisolar calendar adopted by Rabbinic tradition after the exile, which the DSS community and the Orit Ge'ez did not follow. Pesher Habakkuk records that this day's date itself was a point of real conflict between the community and its opponents. Prepare by settling all ordinary matters before sunrise; nothing is eaten, drunk, or worked at from sunrise to the following sunrise. Vayikra 16:21 (the basis Temple Scroll follows) specifies the content of the High Priest's confession over the goat - "all the iniquities of the people of Yisra'EL, and all their transgressions, all their sins" - but not a fixed word-for-word formula; no such wording is preserved in the DSS. (The well-known Hebrew confession text quoted for this day comes from the Mishnah, centuries later and outside this site's sourcing standard, so it is not used here.)

𐤇𐤂 𐤄𐤎𐤊𐤅𐤕 — Chag HaSukkot — Feast of Tabernacles — First day of the seven-day harvest festival. Pilgrimage to the sanctuary. Construction of booths. Celebrated with great joy and abundant sacrifice. Month 7, Day 15 of the 364-day covenant calendar (the seventh month). Kept as: 𐤌𐤅𐤏𐤃 Mo'ed — Appointed Time (Vayikra 23:2); 𐤌𐤒𐤓𐤀 𐤒𐤃𐤔 Miqra Qodesh — Set-Apart Assembly; 𐤔𐤁𐤕𐤅𐤍 Shabbaton — Total Cessation. Begins at sunrise; ends at sunrise the next morning. Source: DSS/Orit.

key_terms.term: Sukkot — First Day — What to Get Ready
key_terms.definition: Gathered before sunrise: Lumber, poles, or a prefab frame for a booth; Palm branches, leafy boughs, or lattice for a partial roof - left open enough to see the sky through; Tarps, fabric, or screening for the walls; Rope or twine.

key_terms.term: Sukkot — First Day — What to Do
key_terms.definition: 1. Build the booth before the festival begins. 2. Live and eat in the booth for the full seven days, not merely visit it. 3. Keep the day as a pilgrimage festival with sacrifice and rejoicing (Vayikra 23:40-43).

Seven days dwelling in booths as a memorial of the wilderness years (Vayikra 23:40-43). Build the booth before the festival begins; live and eat in it, not merely visit it, for the full week. It is kept as a pilgrimage festival with sacrifice and rejoicing. No festival-specific prayer text for this day survives among the primary sources.

𐤇𐤂 𐤄𐤎𐤊𐤅𐤕 — Chag HaSukkot — Final day of Sukkot — The seventh day of the Feast of Tabernacles. Day of great ceremony and water libation. Month 7, Day 21 of the 364-day covenant calendar (the seventh month). Kept as: 𐤌𐤅𐤏𐤃 Mo'ed — Appointed Time (Vayikra 23:2). Begins at sunrise; ends at sunrise the next morning. Source: DSS/Orit.

key_terms.term: Sukkot — Seventh Day — What to Get Ready
key_terms.definition: Gathered before sunrise: Nothing new - the booth built for the first day continues in use.

key_terms.term: Sukkot — Seventh Day — What to Do
key_terms.definition: 1. Continue dwelling in the booth through this final day. 2. Keep this as the last of the seven days of joy, not a separate rite. 3. Leaven and ordinary residence do not resume until this day has passed.

The closing day of dwelling in booths. Leaven and ordinary residence do not resume until this day has passed; the primary sources describe it as the last of the seven days of joy, not a separate rite in itself. No festival-specific prayer text for this day survives among the primary sources.

𐤏𐤑𐤓𐤕 — Atzeret — Eighth Day Assembly — The day after Sukkot. A closing solemn gathering distinct from the seven days of Tabernacles. Confirmed in DSS legal texts. Month 7, Day 22 of the 364-day covenant calendar (the seventh month). Observance follows the Esther narrative itself (Esther 9): fasting beforehand, then feasting and rejoicing at deliverance. The 364th and final day, completing the solar cycle before it turns back to the spring equinox and a new year begins. Chanokh Ch. 79:6 states the year "is accurately completed" by this reckoning - the text presents 364 as whole and correct on its own terms, with no acknowledgment of the further roughly 1.25-day-per-year gap against the true solar year, and no mechanism for correcting one; that question is not addressed in the primary sources. multiple_choice.question: When does an appointed time begin and end?
multiple_choice.source_quote: The verse itself is rendered "evening to evening," but the operative day boundary followed here is sunrise to sunrise, per the DSS/Orit solar reckoning (Yovelim 3:28, 21:10, Vayikra 7:15, 22:29-30, Shemot 12:10, 23:18, 29:34, 34:25, Bamidbar 9:12, Devarim 16:4, 4QCalendrical Texts 4Q320-330) - sunset-to-sunset reckoning follows the Babylonian lunisolar calendar adopted by Rabbinic tradition after the exile, which the DSS community and the Orit Ge'ez did not follow.

Slaughter of the Passover lamb. faq.question: What does the Mo’edim reference give for First Fruits of Barley?

faq.question: What does the Mo’edim reference give for Yom Kippur?
faq.answer: name: Yom Kippur | paleo: 𐤉𐤅𐤌 𐤄𐤊𐤐𐤅𐤓𐤉𐤌 | timing: Month 7, Day 10 | begins: sunrise | ends: sunrise the next morning | what it is: Day of Atonement — The tenth of the seventh month. The High Priest enters the Holy of Holies. Complete fast from sunrise to sunrise. The most solemn day of the sacred year. Confirmed across all DSS legal texts. | to get ready: Nothing to purchase - this is a complete fast from sunrise to sunrise. The preparation is clearing one's calendar and settling ordinary matters beforehand, not acquiring anything. | to do: Before sunrise, settle all ordinary matters and calendar obligations.; At sunrise, begin the complete fast and total rest - self-affliction (inui nefesh), the Torah's own phrase (Vayikra 16, 23:26-32).; Eat, drink, and work at nothing for the full day.; No fixed confession wording survives in the DSS for the High Priest's role (Vayikra 16:21 describes its content, not exact words; the well-known Hebrew confession is Mishnaic and isn't used here).; Continue the fast without interruption through the following sunrise, when it ends. | source: DSS/Orit
